A.explanation: Too small - about $390 \text{ m}$ is less than the area under the $0$ to $14 \text{ s}$ part of the velocity-time graph.

B.explanation: The area under the velocity-time graph from $0$ to about $14 \text{ s}$ is about $570 \text{ m}$, which equals the distance fallen.

C.explanation: Too large - about $710 \text{ m}$ includes extra area after the rapid velocity drop when the parachute is already open.

D.explanation: Too large - about $770 \text{ m}$ is near the area up to $20 \text{ s}$ and so includes falling with the parachute open.

hints: Look at the shape of the velocity-time graph and decide at what time the parachute opens - notice where the velocity stops being steady at $60 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and falls rapidly, near $14 \text{ s}$.
Recall that for a velocity-time graph the distance travelled is the area under the graph, so you need the area from $t = 0$ up to the opening time only.
Estimate that area by counting grid squares where each small square is $1 \text{ s}$ by $2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, or by comparing with triangles and rectangles, and check which option is closest.
walkthrough: Identify when the parachute opens. The velocity rises to $60 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ by about $10 \text{ s}$, stays constant, then drops steeply from about $14 \text{ s}$. So distance before opening is the area under the curve from $0$ to about $14 \text{ s}$.
State the rule: displacement $=$ area under velocity-time graph. Here $s = \int v \, dt$, with $v$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $t$ in $\text{s}$ giving $s$ in $\text{m}$.

Estimate the area. Counting squares: one small square $= 1 \text{ s} \times 2 \text{ m s}^{-1} = 2 \text{ m}$. The area $0$ to $10 \text{ s}$ is roughly $430 \text{ m}$ and the $10 \text{ s}$ to $14 \text{ s}$ rectangle is about $4 \times 60 = 240 \text{ m}$, but the curve is below a full rectangle early on, giving a total of about $550$ to $600 \text{ m}$.
Compare with the options. $390 \text{ m}$ is far too low, while $710 \text{ m}$ and $770 \text{ m}$ require including the area after $14 \text{ s}$ when she is slowing down with the parachute open.
The estimate of about $570 \text{ m}$ matches the area before the rapid drop. This is option B.
